```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)

liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
```
## ARIMA vs ETS
```{r}
#| echo: false
autoplot(liquor, .vars = sales) +
  labs(title = "Monthly US Liquor Sales", y = "Sales (millions of dollars)", x = "Year")

liquor %>%
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot of Monthly US Liquor Sales", y = " Log Sales (millions of dollars)", x = "Month")
```
There is clearly an upwards trend in monthly US liqor sales, along with a seasonal pattern. The summer months have high alcohol sales, but December has the highest sales. The seasonal swings are growing with the level, so using logs would be appropriate.
```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```
ARIMA: It chose an ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] model with drift. This means that it chose one seasonal difference. Two seasonal lags are used for the autoregressive part, and one seasonal lag is used for the moving average part. It chose to do no additional differencing, and it chose to use two non-seasonal moving average lags and one non-seasonal autoregressive lag.

ETS: R specified additive error, trend, and seasonal components on the logged series. It produced a small beta and gamma, meaning that changes in trend and seasonal swings are fairly constant. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```
The residuals do not look like white noise. Reject the null of the ljung-box test at pvalue 0.
```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
216 forecast origins were considered for this TSCV.

First Month: Jan 2002
Last month: December 2019

The ARIMA model is the better model. Both RMSE and MAE are lower.
```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```
ARIMA vs ETS: DM = -2.90, p-val = 0.0040

ARIMA vs SNAIVE: DM = -10.755, p-val = ~0.000

I would chose the ARIMA model, as it performs better by the metric of RMSE and MAE, and the DM test shows that the ARIMA model is significantly better than both ETS and SNAIVE.

## Forecast Combination
```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
the combination is better than ETS on its own, but worse than ARIMA.
```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```
There is large correlation between the errors of ETS and ARIMA. If we could optimally deal with this I would use covariance to reduce the size of a weight. Because the ETS model is significantly worse than the ARIMA model via DM test, I would conclude equal weights
is a bad way to combine these two models.

## BAR vs BVAR
```{r}
#| include: false
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```
There will be 120 forcasts. The first will be Q1 1990 and the last will be Q4 2019
```{r}
#| echo: false
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
```
The VAR(1) forecasts better for 7 of the 8 variables. VAR(4) only does better on inflation. The smaller model does better because the larger model is likely overfitting.
```{r}
#| echo: false
fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
fc_bvar_005 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_005.rds")
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
1)The BVAR(4) with lam=0.3 performs better than the OLS VAR(4) for all variables. The Minnesota prior has the effect of making more distant lags matter less, which has improved the accuracy of the model. The parameters also get shrunk towards 0.

2)The BVAR(1) performs better than BVAR(4) lam=0.3 for 5 of the 8 variables..

3)The BVAR(4) with lam=0.05 performs worse than the BVAR(4) lam=0.3 for all variable but one. There may be too much shrinkage with a lamda that small. RMSE is a fair estimate of how accurately it will forecast in the future assuming future data looks like the data in the test period.
```{r}
#| echo: false
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)


e_var5 <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_var4[, 2]
e_bvar1 <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_bvar_03[, 2]

forecast::dm.test(e_var5, e_bvar1, h = 1, power = 2)
```
I reject the null that BVAR(4) and VAR(4) have equal forecast accuracy for GDP or consumption growth. It doesn't really change my thinking from 4.3b.

## Factor Model
```{r}
#| include: false
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}
```
```{r}
#| echo: false 
fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)

#5.1c
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```
INDPRO and PAYEMS were transformed to growth rates. CPI was transformed to change in growth rate and FEDFUNDS was transformed to first difference.FEDFUNDS doesn't have a trend, whereas INDPRO does. FEDFUNDS is probably auto correlated, so a difference makes sense.
```{r}
#| echo: false
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```
The first three principal components account for 29.4% of the variation.
```{r}
#| echo: false
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

#5.2c
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```
The first PC contains measures of real economic activity. Farm payroll, manufacturing, etc. The second PC contains 8 measures of a price index. It's representing inflation/price level.
```{r}
#| echo: false
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```
Yes, i got the same numbers. It would be cheating to estimate the full factors because you would be encoding future information into your model. In a non-testing environment you don't have future data.
```{r}
#| echo: false
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
```
The factors improve the forecast accuracy. It decreased RMSE by 10.43%. The result is statistically significant.
## Reflection
It was interesting how powerful ARIMA was on its own. ETS couldn't compete, and nor could an equal weights model. Simplicity is hard to beat, I also saw that with the BVAR(1) beating the BVAR(4), but not nearly as bad as the VAR(1) beat the VAR(4). Both of these things speak to the over fitting issues we get with more complicated models. Both the shrinkage from BVAR and the combined factor model helped deal with overfitting.
